chapters.title: Gospel and Evangelise
chapters.subtitle: The gospel is news from the battlefield: the King has won, and he is coming to reign
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew, to “bring good news” (basar) was what a runner did when he raced from the battlefield to tell a city the outcome. Isaiah used this picture for the best news of all: God has won, he is returning, and he reigns. The Greek words euangelion and euangelizomai carry the same idea, and Jesus began his ministry by announcing that this long-awaited reign of God had come near.
chapters.bigIdea: The gospel is first of all an announcement that God, through Jesus the Messiah, has won the victory and now reigns as King.
skeleton: We often think the gospel is a plan for getting to heaven
In Hebrew, basar means to bring news, usually news of victory
Isaiah's herald announces to Zion: “Your God reigns!”
The Septuagint translates this with euangelizomai, “announce good news”
In the Roman world, euangelia announced an emperor's victories and birthday
Jesus announced that God's kingdom had come near; Paul summed up its centre: Christ died, was buried and was raised
To evangelise is to announce the King's victory and invite people to live under his reign

p: For many Christians the word **gospel** means a short explanation of how a person can be forgiven and go to heaven after death. To **evangelise** means to explain that plan and ask someone to accept it. These things matter, and they are part of the story.

But the Bible's words for “gospel” come from a bigger world. They are words of **news**: something has happened, and someone has run to tell you about it. Our English word “gospel” itself comes from the Old English *gōdspel*, “good story” or “good news”. Before it was a plan, the gospel was a report of an event, and especially of a victory.

The Hebrew verb is *basar* (in the form *bisser*), “to bring news”. Usually it is good news, and often it is **news from a battle**. When the Philistines defeated Saul, they sent messengers through their land “to carry the good news” to their temples and people (1 Samuel 31:9). When Absalom's rebellion was crushed, Ahimaaz begged Joab, “Let me run and carry news to the king” (2 Samuel 18:19).

The noun is *besorah*, “news”, and sometimes “a reward for news”. David bitterly recalls the man who thought he was bringing good news about Saul's death, and “that was the reward I gave him for his news” (2 Samuel 4:10). Four starving lepers, finding the enemy camp empty, say to each other, “This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent” (2 Kings 7:9). Good news is meant to be told.

> A quick note: the same three Hebrew letters (ב־שׂ־ר) also spell *basar*, “flesh”. Most lexicons treat these as two separate words that happen to look alike, so we should not build a meaning out of the likeness. The “good news” word stands on its own.

sections.h: Mevasser: the herald on the mountains
p: The one who brings the news is the *mevasser*, the **herald of good news**. Picture a watchman on the city wall. He sees a runner coming over the hills, and everyone holds their breath: have we won or lost? Is the king alive? Is the enemy coming?

Isaiah takes this scene and fills it with God's own victory. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns’” (Isaiah 52:7). The prophet Nahum uses almost the same words for the fall of Nineveh (Nahum 1:15; in Hebrew 2:1).

Earlier Isaiah tells Zion herself to become the herald: “Go up on a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news… say to the cities of Judah, ‘Behold your God!’” (Isaiah 40:9). And the Servant says, “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the poor” (Isaiah 61:1). In Isaiah the good news is simple: **God has won, he is coming back to his people, and he reigns.**

When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they used *euangelizomai*, “to announce good news”, for *basar*. The word is built from *eu* (good) and *angelos* (messenger). So Isaiah's herald in Greek is one who *euangelizetai*, who brings good news.

The New Testament picks up exactly these words. The noun *euangelion* (good news, gospel) appears about 76 times, most of all in Paul. The verb *euangelizomai* is a favourite of Luke. And *euangelistēs*, **evangelist**, means “one who announces good news”: Philip “the evangelist” (Acts 21:8), one of the gifts Christ gives the church (Ephesians 4:11), and Timothy's calling, “do the work of an evangelist” (2 Timothy 4:5).

When Paul wants to show why preachers matter, he quotes Isaiah 52:7 directly: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (Romans 10:15). For Paul, the Christian gospel is the fulfilment of Isaiah's herald on the mountains.

sections.h: Good news in the Roman world
p: The Greek word also had a political meaning. In the Roman Empire, *euangelia* (good news) were announced when the emperor won a war, recovered from illness, came to the throne or had a son. Cities held celebrations and offered sacrifices.

A famous inscription from the city of Priene in Asia Minor (about 9 BC) praises Caesar Augustus as a saviour who brought peace, and says that **the birthday of the god was the beginning of good news (euangelia) for the world** because of him.

So when the first Christians announced “the good news of Jesus Christ”, their hearers would have caught the sound of a royal proclamation. There was another King, and his reign brought a different kind of peace. This helps explain why the message was felt to be not only religious but a challenge to Caesar's claims (compare Acts 17:7).

sections.h: The Jewish hope behind Jesus' message
p: By the time of Jesus, many Jews read Isaiah's good news as the promise that God would finally return as King, end the exile, defeat evil and set his people free. The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah, an ancient Jewish paraphrase read in synagogues, renders “Your God reigns” in Isaiah 52:7 as “**the kingdom of your God has been revealed**”.

One of the Dead Sea Scrolls (known as 11QMelchizedek) also links Isaiah 52:7 with Isaiah 61 and the Jubilee “release”, looking for a messenger anointed by the Spirit who would announce God's day of freedom. Jesus' hearers knew these hopes well.

> This is the background of Jesus' first words in Mark: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). He was not inventing a new idea. He was announcing that Isaiah's long-awaited news was coming true, now.

sections.h: How Jesus and the apostles told the good news
p: Mark opens his book, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ” (Mark 1:1). In Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61, “to bring good news to the poor”, and says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:18–21). He says, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose” (Luke 4:43).

Paul describes “the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets”, about God's Son, “descended from David according to the flesh” and declared Son of God in power by his resurrection (Romans 1:1–4). Here the gospel is the story of the promised Davidic King.

His most famous summary is 1 Corinthians 15:1–4: Christ **died for our sins** in accordance with the Scriptures, he was **buried**, and he was **raised on the third day** in accordance with the Scriptures. Forgiveness of sins is at the heart of it. But it is set inside the larger story: by his death and resurrection Jesus has defeated sin and death and been enthroned as Lord. When Philip met the Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53, “beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35).

A common Western habit is to shrink the gospel into a few steps for individual salvation: you are a sinner, Jesus paid your penalty, pray this prayer, and you will go to heaven. Each step contains truth, but the shape has changed. The news has become mainly a transaction, and the King and his kingdom have faded into the background.

Read in its Jewish setting, the gospel is first an **announcement about God and his Messiah**: the King has won, sin and death are defeated, God's reign has broken into the world. Forgiveness, new life and the hope of resurrection all flow from that victory. The fitting response is to turn (repent), trust the King and live under his reign, now and forever.

The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament use one family of words for good news: *basar* in Hebrew, *euangelizomai* in the Septuagint and the New Testament. But English versions usually split it. In the Old Testament we read “bear tidings” or “bring good news” (2 Samuel 18:19; Isaiah 52:7). In the New Testament we read “preach the gospel” (Luke 4:18). Translators follow the familiar wording of each part of the Bible, and “gospel” has a long Christian history. The result is that readers rarely notice that Jesus and Paul are using Isaiah's word.

The Latin chain added another layer. The Vulgate did not translate *euangelion*; it borrowed it as *evangelium*. Western languages kept the loanword, so we have “evangelist”, “evangelical” and “evangelise”: technical church words. English did translate it once, as *gōdspel*, “good news”, but over a thousand years “gospel” itself became a technical word too, used for a book, a style of music and a summary of doctrine. Some modern versions try to recover the plain sense by writing “good news” (for example the Good News Bible).

One more small loss: in Isaiah 61:1 the KJV says “good tidings unto the meek”. The Hebrew *anavim* means the poor and the afflicted, people pressed down by life. “Meek” sounds like a gentle personality. Most modern versions say “the poor”, which matches Jesus' reading in Luke 4:18 and reminds us that this news was first good news for the oppressed.

In Israel, news travelled on foot. After a battle, runners raced home; watchmen on the city wall looked out and tried to read the runner's pace and style (2 Samuel 18:24–27). The whole city waited. A messenger with good news could expect a reward, which is one meaning of *besorah*, while bad news could be dangerous to bring. Jewish tradition still has a blessing for hearing good news: “Blessed is He who is good and does good” (Mishnah Berakhot 9:2).

Most people could not read, so news, laws and Scripture were all spoken aloud: in the market, at the city gate and in the synagogue. The good news about Jesus was first an oral announcement, told and retold by witnesses, before it was written down. Only later did the word “gospel” come to be used as the name of the four books that record that news.

In the Roman world, *euangelia* had the sound of the imperial court. When news of a victory or an emperor's accession arrived, cities held festivals, offered sacrifices and put up inscriptions. The herald represented the ruler, so to welcome his news was to welcome the ruler's reign, and to reject it was a kind of rebellion. Against that background, the Christian announcement of another King, crucified and raised, was both joyful and bold.

If the gospel is news, then to **evangelise** is to be a herald, not a salesperson. A herald does not invent the message or argue people into it with tricks. He tells clearly and joyfully what has happened, and invites people to respond to the King.

It also means the good news is meant to be seen as well as heard. Isaiah 61 and Luke 4 include good news for the poor, release for captives and sight for the blind. When followers of Jesus forgive, heal, feed and set people free, they show what the King's reign looks like. Like the lepers in 2 Kings 7, we cannot keep silent: “This day is a day of good news.”

chapters.title: Preach and Proclaim
chapters.subtitle: Biblical preaching is a herald calling out the King's news, then reading, explaining and reasoning together
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew, to proclaim (qara) is to call out loud, like announcing the Jubilee or Jonah crying out in Nineveh. In Greek, to preach (kēryssō) is to act as a herald who announces a king's decree. In the synagogue, God's word was read aloud, explained and applied, and people discussed it. Biblical preaching combines a bold announcement of what God has done with patient reading, explanation and conversation.
chapters.bigIdea: To preach is to announce God's news as a herald and to open the Scriptures so that people understand and respond.
skeleton: We often picture preaching as one person lecturing from a pulpit
Hebrew qara means to call out: proclaim liberty, cry out a message
Ezra's reading “gave the sense” so the people understood
Greek kēryssō is the work of a herald announcing a king's decree
Synagogues read the Law and the Prophets, then gave a word of exhortation
Jesus and Paul proclaimed, read, explained and reasoned with people
Preaching today: bold announcement plus open Scripture and real conversation

p: When we hear **preach**, many of us picture a pastor standing in a pulpit, speaking for half an hour while everyone else listens quietly. In everyday English, “don't preach at me” even means “don't lecture me about how to behave”.

The Bible's words paint a wider picture. Some of them are about **calling out an announcement**, like a town crier. Some are about **reading and explaining** God's word so people understand. Others are about **reasoning and discussing** together. To see what biblical preaching is, we need all of these words, Hebrew and Greek.

The basic Hebrew verb is *qara*, “to call, call out, proclaim”. It is used for calling someone's name, for crying out to God, and for **proclaiming a public announcement**. It is a loud, public word: something is called out so that everyone can hear it and respond.

At the Jubilee, Israel was told: “You shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants” (Leviticus 25:10). Isaiah's anointed messenger is sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives… to proclaim the year of the LORD's favour” (Isaiah 61:1–2). Proclaiming here is not giving advice; it is announcing that something new is now true: debts are cancelled and slaves go free.

God told Jonah, “Arise, go to Nineveh… and call out against it the message (*qeri'ah*) that I tell you” (Jonah 3:2). Jonah walked into the city and cried out, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!” (Jonah 3:4). The prophet did not make up the message. He called out what God gave him.

sections.h: Miqra and Qohelet: reading to the gathered people
p: From *qara* comes *miqra*, a “calling together” or “reading”. In the Torah it describes a *miqra qodesh*, a “holy convocation”, when the people were called to gather before God (Leviticus 23:2). In Nehemiah 8:8 it means the public reading of Scripture. Later Jews came to call the whole Hebrew Bible *Miqra*, “that which is read aloud”.

The book of Ecclesiastes is spoken by *Qohelet* (Ecclesiastes 1:1), often translated “the Preacher”. The word comes from *qahal*, “assembly”, so it means one who gathers or speaks to an assembly. The Greek title *Ecclesiastes* comes from *ekklēsia*, the same word later used for “church”. Biblical preaching belongs to **a gathered community**, not to a lonely voice.

Prophets also spoke God's word in public. The verb *niba* (to prophesy) is used when God tells Amos, “Go, prophesy to my people Israel” (Amos 7:15), and Ezekiel, “Prophesy over these bones” (Ezekiel 37:4). Prophecy often meant speaking God's word into the present situation, calling people back to the covenant.

A key scene comes after the exile. Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform and read the Torah to all the people from early morning until midday. The Levites “read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). They **helped the people understand** (Nehemiah 8:7). Jewish tradition later saw this as the beginning of the practice of translating and explaining the Scripture reading in the synagogue.

Ezra “had set his heart to study (*darash*, seek) the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach” it (Ezra 7:10). From *darash* comes later Hebrew *derashah*, a sermon or exposition: preaching that grows out of searching the text deeply.

sections.h: Kēryssō: the herald of the King
p: The main Greek word for preach is *kēryssō*, “to proclaim as a herald”. In the Greek world a *kēryx* (herald) was an official messenger. He announced a king's decree, a city's decision, a truce or the start of public games. His task was to deliver the message **faithfully and loudly**, not to add his own opinions.

The Septuagint uses *kēryssō* for Hebrew *qara*. In Isaiah 61:1 the messenger is sent “to proclaim (*kēryxai*) release to the captives”, the very words Jesus reads in Luke 4:18–19. The message itself is the *kērygma*, “the proclamation” (1 Corinthians 1:21; Romans 16:25). Jesus says Nineveh “repented at the preaching (*kērygma*) of Jonah” (Matthew 12:41).

Two related words widen the picture. *Katangellō* means to announce or make known: “What you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23). And the whole church does it at the Lord's table: “you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Paul calls himself “a preacher (*kēryx*) and an apostle” (1 Timothy 2:7), and Peter calls Noah “a herald of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5).

Preaching in Acts is not only announcement. Luke often uses *dialegomai*, “to reason, discuss, have a dialogue” (the root of our word “dialogue”). In Thessalonica Paul went into the synagogue “as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures” (Acts 17:2). In Corinth “he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath” (Acts 18:4). At Troas he “talked with” the believers until midnight (Acts 20:7). This was **a conversation with questions and answers**, not only a speech.

The early believers also spoke with *parrēsia*, “boldness, freedom of speech”, literally “saying everything”. The leaders were amazed at “the boldness of Peter and John”, ordinary men who had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13). The church prayed, “Grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness” (Acts 4:29). Boldness is not harshness; it is speaking openly because the message is true.

In Jesus' day, synagogue gatherings centred on **reading Scripture aloud**. There was a reading from the Law (Torah) and a reading from the Prophets, and then someone might give a teaching. In Pisidian Antioch, “after the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, ‘Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it’” (Acts 13:15). Paul stood up and preached. James could even say that Moses “is proclaimed in every city, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues” (Acts 15:21).

In Nazareth Jesus stood up to read, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, read Isaiah 61, rolled it up, sat down (the usual posture of a teacher), and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). Then the people responded, questioned and argued. The reading of the word, a short explanation and the community's response all belonged together.

> Jesus' own preaching was a herald's announcement: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17; Mark 1:14–15). He proclaimed the news, and then explained it with parables, questions and conversations, at tables, on hillsides and in homes as well as in synagogues.

One Western habit is to see preaching mainly as a **moral lecture**: being told to try harder. Another is to see it as a **performance** by one gifted professional while others watch. A third is to think preaching is only for the pulpit, and has nothing to do with ordinary believers.

Through the Jewish lens, preaching is first **news**: the herald announces what God has done in the Messiah (see the study on the gospel). It is rooted in the **public reading of Scripture**, carefully explained so people understand. It welcomes **reasoning and questions**. And the whole community proclaims, at the Lord's table, in daily speech and in life. Many scholars distinguish *kērygma* (proclamation) from *didachē* (teaching), though in practice the New Testament joins them closely.

The English word “preach” comes from the Latin *praedicare*, “to proclaim publicly”. In the Vulgate it translates *kēryssō*, and English Bibles followed. At first “preach” kept that public, announcing sense. Over centuries it narrowed to a church sermon, and even to moralising: “don't preach at me”. So when we read that Jesus “preached”, we tend to picture a pulpit rather than a herald calling out the King's news in the open air.

The KJV also uses “preach” for several different Greek words: *kēryssō* (herald), *euangelizomai* (announce good news), *katangellō* (make known), *laleō* (speak) and even *dialegomai* (discuss), as in Acts 20:7, “Paul preached unto them”, where modern versions say “talked with them”. Translators in 1611 chose a familiar church word, and it reads smoothly. But it flattens the variety: announcing, telling news, speaking and reasoning together all become one activity.

The title of Ecclesiastes is a good example of the chain from Hebrew to English. *Qohelet* means one who gathers or speaks to an assembly. The Septuagint called him *Ekklēsiastēs*, “one who speaks in the assembly”; the Latin kept that name; and the KJV made him “the Preacher”. The NIV says “the Teacher”. Each choice is reasonable, but none quite captures a wise person speaking to a gathered community.

In Israel, important things were called out in public. The Jubilee began with the shofar sounded through the land (Leviticus 25:9). Jeremiah was told, “Stand in the gate of the LORD's house, and proclaim there this word” (Jeremiah 7:2). Prophets, heralds and town elders spoke where people gathered: at the city gate, in the Temple courts, at the market. Preaching in this world was loud, public and meant for everyone.

In the synagogue, the reader stood and the teacher sat (Luke 4:16, 20). Because many people understood Aramaic better than Hebrew, a translator rendered the reading aloud, verse by verse, and the Mishnah sets rules for how this was done (Mishnah Megillah 4:4). After the reading, there was explanation, and often discussion. Jewish learning loved questions, which is why the boy Jesus is found in the Temple “listening to them and asking them questions” (Luke 2:46).

The Greco-Roman world knew two kinds of public speaker. The herald (*kēryx*) was a sacred official messenger who carried a staff and was not to be harmed; he spoke someone else's message. The orator was trained in rhetoric to impress and persuade, and was often paid. Paul deliberately places himself with the herald, not the orator: “I did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom… my message and my preaching were not in plausible words” (1 Corinthians 2:1–4).

If you preach or teach, remember you are a herald: your job is to deliver the King's message faithfully, not your own opinions. Read the Scripture clearly, give the sense, and leave room for questions. If you listen to preaching, come like the Bereans, who “received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily” (Acts 17:11).

And all of us can proclaim. Paul asks, “How are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15). Whether in a pulpit, a kitchen or a workplace, we can boldly and gently call out the good news: the kingdom of God has come near.

words.note: Used for announcing the Jubilee and for Jonah's cry in Nineveh.
words.missed: Bibles render qara as “call”, “cry”, “proclaim”, “read” or “preach”, so the one loud, public action behind them is hidden.
words.culture: Public announcements were cried out at the city gate or the Temple, and the Jubilee was opened with a blast of the shofar (Leviticus 25:9).

words.note: The message God gave Jonah to call out.
words.missed: The KJV's “preach the preaching” keeps the wordplay but adds a pulpit picture that the Hebrew does not have.
words.culture: Nineveh was a huge city; a prophet walking its streets crying out a short message was a public event everyone could hear.

words.note: Later the Jewish name for the whole Hebrew Bible, “what is read aloud”.
words.missed: “Holy convocation” and “reading” sound like two different things; in Hebrew both are a “calling out”.
words.culture: Festivals gathered the people at a call, and Scripture was heard aloud in the assembly, not read silently at home.

words.gloss: one who speaks to an assembly, “the Preacher”
words.note: From qahal, assembly; the Greek title Ecclesiastes comes from ekklēsia.
words.missed: “The Preacher” comes through Greek and Latin and suggests a pulpit; the Hebrew title is about gathering an assembly.
words.culture: Wisdom in Israel was taught to gatherings at the gate, in the court or among students, by older and wiser speakers.

words.note: Speaking God's word into the present situation.
words.missed: “Prophesy” today sounds like predicting the future; niba is mostly speaking God's word into the present.
words.culture: Prophets often spoke in public places, the Temple courts or the king's court, and their words could put them in danger.

words.note: Ezra set his heart to seek the Torah, do it and teach it.
words.missed: “Seek” or “study” misses that darash means searching a text or God with your whole life, to obey.
words.culture: Scribes like Ezra copied, studied and taught the Torah; searching Scripture was a respected life's work.

words.note: A sermon that grows out of searching the text.
words.missed: Not in English Bibles; “sermon” suggests a speech, but derashah is exposition that grows from close reading.
words.culture: In synagogue a teacher would sit and explain the reading, often linking verses together by catchwords.

words.note: The Septuagint's word for qara in Isaiah 61:1.
words.missed: “Preach” makes kēryssō sound like a church talk; the Greek is a herald calling out an official announcement.
words.culture: Greek cities used heralds for public decrees, truces and games; their voice carried the authority of the city or king.

words.note: An official messenger who delivers a king's decree faithfully.
words.missed: “Preacher” suggests a pastor; a kēryx was an official messenger, often protected even in war.
words.culture: Heralds carried a staff (the kērykeion) as a sign that they were sacred messengers who must not be harmed.

words.note: The content of what the herald announces.
words.missed: The KJV's “the foolishness of preaching” can point to the act or style; kērygma is mainly the content announced.
words.culture: In public life a kērygma was the herald's proclamation itself: the decree that everyone must hear and obey.

words.note: The whole church proclaims the Lord's death at his table.
words.missed: “Shew” or “proclaim” are fine, but readers may miss that this is about announcing news openly.
words.culture: Athens was full of people sharing new ideas in the market; Paul “proclaims” there an unknown God made known (Acts 17:23).

words.note: Paul's custom in the synagogues: reasoning from the Scriptures.
words.missed: The KJV twice turns dialegomai into “preached” (Acts 20:7, 9), hiding that it was a dialogue.
words.culture: Philosophers in the Greek agora debated with question and answer, and synagogues welcomed discussion of the readings.

words.note: Literally “saying everything”: speaking openly because the message is true.
words.missed: “Boldness” can sound like being loud or harsh; parrēsia is the frank, open speech of a free person.
words.culture: In Greek cities parrēsia was a citizen's right to speak freely in the assembly; slaves did not have it.

rows.literal: the words of Qohelet (the one who gathers / speaks to an assembly)
rows.why: The title is rare, so the KJV followed the Greek and Latin “Ecclesiastes”; the NIV's “the Teacher” is another guess at the same idea.

rows.literal: and call out to it the calling-out
rows.common: and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV keeps the Hebrew wordplay but uses “preach”; the ESV's “call out against it the message” keeps the street-crier picture.

rows.common: to preach deliverance to the captives (KJV)
rows.why: In Isaiah 61:1 the KJV says “proclaim liberty”; in Luke's quotation it says “preach”, so a Jubilee announcement starts to sound like a sermon.

rows.literal: Paul was discussing / talking with them
rows.why: To 1611 readers this was natural, but it turns a long conversation into a speech; the ESV says “talked with them”.

rows.literal: through the foolishness of the proclamation (what is announced)
rows.why: Readers may think preaching as a method is foolish; Paul means the message of a crucified Messiah, so the ESV says “the folly of what we preach”.

diagrams.title: A synagogue gathering in Jesus' day

steps.d: The community assembles on the Sabbath.
A portion of the Torah is read aloud.
A passage from the Prophets follows (Isaiah 61 in Nazareth).
A teacher sits and explains and applies the reading.
The people ask, discuss, agree or argue.

left.label: Common Western assumption
items: A moral lecture: try harder
One professional speaks, others watch
One-way talk with no questions
Only for the pulpit
The preacher's ideas and opinions

right.label: Jewish lens
items: A herald's news: God has acted
The gathered community hears and responds
Reading, explaining and reasoning together
The whole church proclaims in word and life
The King's message delivered faithfully

verses.text: You shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.
They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.
From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it.
Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures.
How are they to hear without someone preaching?

keyPoints: Hebrew qara means to call out or proclaim, as with the Jubilee and Jonah's message.
Ezra's reading “gave the sense” so the people understood (Nehemiah 8:8).
Greek kēryssō is the work of a herald faithfully announcing a king's decree.
The kērygma is the message itself: God's news in the Messiah.
Synagogues read the Law and the Prophets, then gave a word of exhortation (Acts 13:15).
Paul reasoned (dialegomai) from the Scriptures with questions and discussion.
Biblical preaching joins bold announcement, clear explanation and real conversation.
reflect: When you think of preaching, do you picture a lecture, a performance, or a herald's announcement?
How could your church or group make more room for reading Scripture aloud, explaining it and discussing it?
Where could you speak about Jesus this week with both boldness and gentleness?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew verb qara basically mean?
quiz.why: Qara is used for proclaiming liberty (Leviticus 25:10) and calling out a message (Jonah 3:2).

quiz.q: What did the Levites do in Nehemiah 8:8?
options: Read the Law clearly and gave the sense
quiz.why: They read and explained so that the people understood the reading.

quiz.q: In the Greek world, what was a kēryx?
options: A herald who announced official messages
quiz.why: The herald delivered the king's message faithfully, without adding his own ideas.

quiz.q: What happened in the synagogue after the reading of the Law and the Prophets in Acts 13:15?
options: A word of encouragement was invited
quiz.why: The rulers invited Paul and his companions to give a word of exhortation.

quiz.q: What does dialegomai, used of Paul in Acts 17:2, mean?
quiz.why: Paul reasoned with people from the Scriptures, in dialogue.

quiz.q: In Acts 20:7 the KJV says Paul “preached unto them”. What does the Greek verb dialegomai suggest?
options: He talked and reasoned with them in conversation
quiz.why: Dialegomai means to discuss or reason (the root of “dialogue”); modern versions say “talked with them”.

terms.def: Hebrew verb, to call, call out, proclaim.
Assembly or reading; later the Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible.
The speaker of Ecclesiastes, “the Preacher”: one who speaks to an assembly.
Later Hebrew word for a sermon or exposition, from darash, to seek.
Greek verb, to proclaim as a herald.
The proclamation: the message the herald announces.
Greek verb, to reason or discuss; the root of “dialogue”.
Boldness, freedom of speech; literally “saying everything”.
